lines.source: old lab film, scene 1 (the negative gradient is the learning signal)
lines.text: How does a machine actually learn? It walks downhill.

lines.source: loss landscape: a loss L over the parameters
lines.text: Picture every possible version of a model as a point on a landscape. Height is how wrong that version is. Learning means finding low ground.

lines.source: gradient descent: step against the gradient, repeat
lines.text: But it can't see the landscape. It can only feel the slope under its feet. So it takes a step downhill, feels again, and repeats. Billions of times.

lines.source: step size: too small a learning rate wastes the run
lines.text: Everything depends on the size of that step. Too small, and it crawls.

lines.source: step size: above 2 over the largest curvature the iteration diverges
lines.text: Too large, and it overshoots the valley. Each bounce is bigger than the last, until it flies off.

lines.source: ill-conditioning: a long narrow valley makes plain descent zigzag
lines.text: The hard places are long, narrow valleys. Plain downhill steps zigzag between the walls, and barely move forward.

lines.source: heavy-ball momentum (Polyak 1964): opposing components cancel, the consistent one accumulates
lines.text: The fix is momentum: give the walker a memory of its recent steps. The side to side wobble cancels out, and the forward motion adds up.

lines.source: saddle points dominate in high dimensions under the random-field model (Dauphin et al. 2014)
lines.text: And with millions of dimensions, the traps are rarely pits. They are saddles: flat places that rise one way and fall another. Momentum, and a little noise, help the walker slide off.

lines.source: the author's view; the training trajectory is what Proof-of-Learning records
lines.text: Every AI system you have used was trained this way: a long walk downhill, one small step at a time. And that walk is what my research records, to prove a model was really trained.
